Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Losing energy can increase temperature With negligible surface pressure, virial equilibrium gives E = K+W = −K. Losing energy makes E more negative and can increase kinetic energy and temperature: self-gravity permits negative heat capacity. K=32NkBT, C≡dEdT=−32NkB (negligible surface pressure) Outward heat flow can further heat and contract the core, increasing the temperature difference and reinforcing transport. Negative heat capacity alone does not imply immediate collapse of every gravitating system. 02Specify the constraints before asking about stability The classical model confines mass M inside a spherical box of radius R. It differs from a fixed-pressure Bonnor–Ebert sphere. A fixed-temperature bath and an insulating fixed-energy wall also lead to different stability criteria. Point-particle gravity admits arbitrarily concentrated configurations, so there is no global entropy maximum without short-distance regularization. Stability here concerns local or metastable smooth mean-field equilibria. 03Add an energy scale to the isothermal sphere Integrate the same ψ,m,ξ equations used for Bonnor–Ebert spheres to a box boundary ξb, with ρ = ρc exp(−ψ). This sequence instead compares equilibria at fixed M and R. u=ξ³e−ψm, v=mξ, η≡GMRcs²=v Wall pressure Pb means E = −K no longer applies. Use 2K+W = 3PbV and K = 3Mcₛ²/2 to obtain the energy. E=4πR³Pb−32Mcs²=Mcs²(u−32) Λ≡−ERGM²=3/2−uv 04Locate two different turning points The first maximum of η occurs near ξb = 8.99 and contrast 32.1. The first maximum of Λ is near ξb = 34.4, contrast 709 and Λ = 0.335. Their identification with the first fixed-temperature and fixed-energy stability limits uses supplied thermodynamic/perturbation results. Moving along this sequence is not time evolution. Equilibria have different energies and temperatures at fixed M,R; the selected ensemble specifies perturbation constraints. Contrasts 14, 32.1 and 709 refer to distinct boundary/thermodynamic conditions. 05Connect to core collapse in real clusters In a cluster, two-body relaxation transports energy. A core losing heat can contract, raise its density and accelerate relaxation, driving core collapse. This is not the same timescale as collisionless orbital instability. Hard binaries can release binding energy during encounters, halting collapse and contributing to post-collapse expansion or oscillation. Tides and mass loss matter in open systems; 709 is not a direct observational classifier for real clusters. The panel recomputes boxed isothermal equilibria and stability landmarks. It does not simulate binary formation, a time-dependent core collapse, or paper particle data. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For a boxed isothermal sphere with density contrast 100, distinguish fixed-temperature from fixed-total-energy stability. Show the answer and reasoning 100 exceeds 32.1 but is below 709: it lies beyond the first fixed-M,R,T stability limit but before the fixed-M,R,E limit for a local entropy maximum. These boxed-model values do not directly classify an open star cluster. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
